source.title: Improving Generalization Performance by Switching from Adam to SGD

record.tranche_reason: Compares Adam and SGD on held-out performance and tests whether switching from Adam to SGD closes the observed gap; it does not reproduce the original comparison method exactly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports optimizer comparisons and switching results. Cited results from Wilson et al. and other prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out performance under Adam, SGD and hybrid training with tuned learning rates. Its own image-classification and word-level language-modeling results bear on V4. It is an original source for V4, so no verdict labels are assigned.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: SWATS performs almost as well as the better of Adam and SGD across the reported tasks, often retaining Adam's rapid initial progress. Adam is better than SGD on the word-level language tasks, where SWATS reaches comparable lowest validation perplexity. Switching can temporarily degrade performance.
record.recipe_differences: Tests Adam versus SGD on standard benchmarks, then tests an automatic hybrid that switches from Adam to SGD; reports tuned learning rates and architecture-recommended regularization.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies by modality: Adam is worse than SGD on image-classification tasks but outperforms SGD on word-level language modeling. Manual switch timing also matters on DenseNet/CIFAR-10: switching after 10 epochs gives a learning curve similar to SGD, while switching after 80 epochs gives inferior testing accuracy of ≈ 6.5%.
record.problems: Many optimizer-comparison values are presented only in figures without exact text values. Optimizer learning rates were tuned, but the authors do not report uncertainty estimates. The language-modeling comparison uses lowest validation perplexity.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant results omitted. Manual switch-timing results are described in Figure 2 but not added as separate rows because the row set already captures the tested optimizer comparison and SWATS outcomes; the text reports switch-after-10 and switch-after-80 results, including ≈ 6.5% testing accuracy after switching at 80 epochs.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width-dependent training interpolation and held-out error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local connectivity.

Broader hyperparameter tuning and decoupled weight decay are not experimentally compared. Other adaptive optimizers receive no systematic benchmark comparison. Equal or better final training performance is not documented by the recorded held-out curves.
Effects of adding or removing dropout.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples.

missing.what: SWATS versus Adam and SGD held-out outcomes for all eight CIFAR architecture and dataset combinations. The record omits these central tests of switching-based recovery; Section 3 states that SWATS approaches the better optimizer across tasks.
Direct Adam versus SGD comparison on ResNet-18/Tiny-ImageNet. R11 records only SWATS versus Adam, while the text explicitly includes Tiny-ImageNet among image datasets where Adam generalizes poorly.
The authors report that AMSGrad generalizes similarly to Adam on problems exhibiting an Adam–SGD gap. Record this as a qualitative result with unspecified individual conditions.
Preliminary CIFAR-10 experiments reportedly improve slightly when switching back from SGD to Adam at the end of 300 epochs. No numerical improvement or uncertainty is supplied.

record.verdict_notes: V4 labels are suppressed because arXiv:1712.07628 is one of its original sources. The language-modeling exception already belongs to V4 and should not be labeled a challenge. Learning rates were tuned with other architecture settings largely fixed; SGD's momentum use was also compared, and language-model gradient clipping differed by optimizer. Figure traces are unavailable in the supplied text, so precise figure-only values cannot be verified. Manual switch-timing results are already declared in rows_left_out; their approximately 6.5% value should be described as testing error.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of fixed random labels and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold and test error as a function of width.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the role of local connectivity.

Broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, and whether Adam can do better on word-level language models are not systematically tested. The paper does compare Adam and SGD on language tasks and reports that Adam performs better there.
Dropout effects on held-out error and interaction with data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the generalization gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet-32
rows.operation_detail: Compared Adam and SGD testing error on CIFAR-10.
rows.value: Adam: figure only; authors state Adam stagnates around ≈ 7% error while SGD converges to expected testing error of ≈ 5%.
rows.note: The figure does not provide recoverable exact values for this architecture; the text's specific ≈ 7% versus ≈ 5% comparison describes DenseNet in Section 2.
rows.check: Adam's poorer image generalization agrees with V4. Remove the approximately 7% versus 5% values: those describe DenseNet in Figure 1, not ResNet-32.

rows.subject: DenseNet
rows.operation_detail: Compared Adam and SGD testing error on CIFAR-10.
rows.note: The paper states that Adam's learning-rate schedule fine-tuning did not improve this result.
rows.check: Approximately 7% Adam error versus 5% SGD error is the effect V4 describes, not its reversal. This is the 200-epoch Section 2 experiment.

rows.subject: DenseNet
rows.operation_detail: Used Adam-Clip(1, ∞), which lower-bounds Adam's per-parameter step sizes.
rows.note: The authors say this partially closes the generalization gap.
rows.check: The approximately 6% value is testing error, despite the text calling it accuracy. Lower-bounding Adam's steps narrows but does not close the gap to approximately 5% SGD error.

rows.subject: DenseNet
rows.operation_detail: Used Adam-Clip(0, 1), which upper-bounds Adam's per-parameter step sizes.
rows.value: No tangible effect on final generalization performance
rows.check: Absent describes the clipping intervention's improvement, not V4's optimizer gap. Upper-bounding Adam's steps leaves its worse generalization essentially unchanged.

rows.operation_detail: Compared Adam with SWATS, which switches from Adam to SGD.
rows.value: SWATS: figure only; better peak testing accuracy than Adam, after accuracy drops from 80% to 52% immediately after switching and later recovers.
rows.note: The paper reports a temporary degradation after switching and a better peak than Adam; the figure does not give recoverable final values.
rows.check: SWATS eventually exceeds Adam's peak accuracy, but this row does not establish complete recovery to SGD performance. The 80% to 52% decline is temporary, not a final accuracy comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Own image-classification and language-modeling experiments directly compare held-out performance under Adam, SGD and SWATS.

tranche.reason: The automatic hybrid optimizer provides a different method for investigating optimizer-dependent generalization, with direct Adam and SGD comparisons.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion paraphrase is accurate; no verdicts are listed because this is an original V4 source. Language experiments clip SGD gradients but not Adam or SWATS gradients; exact performance values are not recoverable from the extracted curves.

statements.correction: Tiny-ImageNet: temporary accuracy decline from 80% to 52%, followed by a peak above Adam. Language modeling: Adam outperforms SGD; SWATS achieves comparable lowest validation perplexity to Adam.
statements.problem: R17 establishes comparable lowest validation perplexity, not a worse best result than Adam. Worsening is supported explicitly as temporary degradation after switching.
